# Repository technical analysis and architecture audit

> **Evidence:** This audit analyzes the actual repository codebase, configuration files, and infrastructure manifests on branch `docs/roadmap-playbook`. It documents verified starting conditions and guides the modular monolith migration.

## Repository baseline inventory

An inspection of the repository root, source directories, and configuration files reveals the baseline application state:

| Component path | Technology and frameworks | Observed implementation status | Target resolution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `services/*` (7 services) | Spring Boot 4.0.8, Java 21 | Minimal startup boilerplate; zero domain controllers, entities, or business services. | Consolidate into `services/hrflow-app` modular monolith domain packages. |
| `libs/hrflow-contracts` | Maven, Apache Avro | Avro schema files for attendance check-in; no compiled Java classes. | Defer Avro/Kafka runtime; use JSON outbox payloads in PostgreSQL. |
| `libs/hrflow-event-starter` | Spring Boot autoconfig, Kafka | Kafka producer/consumer template wrappers; no active integration tests. | Superseded by local Spring ApplicationEvent or direct outbox dispatcher. |
| `web/` | Nuxt 3, Vue 3, TypeScript | Default web starter template with basic routing; zero HR business views. | Retain in Git history; develop production web dashboard in React. |
| `ml/confidence-service` | Python 3.12, scikit-learn, FastAPI | Standalone attendance confidence scoring script; passing unit tests. | Deferred from MVP; core attendance rules rely on shift policies and HR review. |
| `infra/docker/` | Docker Compose, PostgreSQL, Kafka | Compose file defining Postgres, Zookeeper, Kafka, Schema Registry, Redis. | Replace with lightweight Compose: PostgreSQL 16, Caddy, Uptime Kuma. |

## Technical inconsistencies and architectural debt

The audit identified several technical discrepancies that must be reconciled during early roadmap phases:

- Build inheritance conflicts: The root `pom.xml` declares Spring Boot parent 4.1.1, while individual service pom files reference 4.0.8. Gateway declares Spring Cloud 2025.1.3. These must be aligned under a unified parent in `services/hrflow-app`.
- Missing database migrations: No Flyway or Liquibase migration scripts exist in any service. The initial schema exists only as proposed DDL in historical documentation.
- Missing business tests: Running `mvn test` in the reactor fails due to missing cached Avro dependencies and nonexistent test classes. There are zero unit or integration tests for attendance, leave, or multi-tenant security.
- Docker Compose mount defects: The existing `docker-compose.yaml` mounts a nonexistent `postgres-init.sql` script and includes invalid listener configuration for Schema Registry.
- Resource headroom limitations: Host system inspection indicates approximately 5 GiB of available disk space and 16 GiB of RAM. Running seven JVM services alongside Kafka and Schema Registry would exhaust memory and cause container crashes.

## Verified command execution record

The following verification commands were executed directly against the workspace to establish ground truth:

```bash
# Maven reactor validation (offline)
mvn -o validate
# Observed result: Ten reactor projects passed syntax validation; no Java compilation performed.
```

```bash
# Nuxt web frontend build check
npm --prefix web run build
# Observed result: Build succeeded for default Nuxt template; no business views present.
```

```bash
# Python machine learning prototype tests
python3 -m pytest -q ml/confidence-service
# Observed result: 5 passed, 1 warning; prototype only, not integrated.
```

```bash
# Compose configuration syntax check
docker compose -f infra/docker/docker-compose.yaml config --quiet
# Observed result: Configuration syntax valid; does not test runtime startup.
```

## Migration path to modular monolith

The findings confirm that the seven-service architecture represents planned scaffolding rather than running production software. Consequently, consolidating into a modular monolith (ADR 006) carries zero regression risk for business features:

1. Create `services/hrflow-app` with domain package boundaries: `identityorg`, `attendance`, `leave`, `request`, `notification`, `reporting`.
1. Establish Flyway migrations for six discrete database schemas in PostgreSQL 16.
1. Implement the Transactional Outbox pattern in `notification.outbox_events` to replace external message brokers.
1. Deploy a private Caddy gateway to handle internal routing and integrate Cloudflare Tunnel for secure remote access.
1. Preserve existing service directories in Git history to maintain provenance without impeding modular development.

# HRFlow engineering documentation handbook

> **Navigation:** [Root README](../README.md) · [Source of truth](SOURCE-OF-TRUTH.md) · [Start here](roadmap/START-HERE.md) · [Dashboard](roadmap/YOU-ARE-HERE.md)

## Introduction and system identity

HRFlow is an event-driven, multi-tenant human resources management platform designed specifically for small-to-medium enterprises and organizations operating under strict data sovereignty, privacy, and budget constraints.

The system provides end-to-end workforce lifecycle automation: company organization structures, employee records, tamper-resistant shift attendance, concurrent leave reservation and approval, general material requests, in-app notifications, and comprehensive audit reporting.

## Core problems solved

Traditional HR software presents serious trade-offs for resource-constrained organizations. Commercial SaaS solutions impose recurring per-user fees, store sensitive personal employee data on third-party cloud infrastructure, and require high-bandwidth continuous internet connectivity. Conversely, manual spreadsheets and legacy custom scripts create data duplication, untracked attendance disputes, race conditions in leave balances, and zero auditability.

HRFlow resolves these problems through three architectural guarantees:

- Absolute tenant isolation: Multi-tenant data residency enforced by verified JWT claims, mandatory tenant foreign keys, composite unique constraints, and strict database schema separation.
- Resilient self-hosting: Packaged as a lightweight Docker Compose deployment suitable for existing on-premises hardware, requiring zero paid cloud databases or Kubernetes clusters.
- Atomic domain consistency: Concurrency-safe transactions, deterministic pessimistic row locking for leave balances, append-only attendance evidence, and an in-database Transactional Outbox.

## User roles and system actors

HRFlow serves four primary human actors and one background automated system:

| Role | Responsibilities | Key capabilities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Employee | Daily workforce member | Check in and out, view shift status, submit leave requests, request workplace equipment. |
| Manager | Team leader and direct supervisor | Review and approve attendance corrections, approve or reject leave requests, inspect team calendars. |
| HR Administrator | Company policy and compliance manager | Configure organization units, job titles, shift policies, public holidays, and export compliance CSVs. |
| Platform Operator | System administrator | Manage Docker Compose, execute nightly backups, verify scratch restores, manage Cloudflare tunnels. |
| System Worker | Automated background processor | Poll transactional outbox, dispatch event receipts, compute attendance summaries, deliver notifications. |

## Minimum Viable Product scope

The initial production release delivers a complete, cohesive walking skeleton across six essential functional domains:

- Identity and organization: Multi-tenant tenant onboarding, user authentication via short-lived JWTs and rotating refresh tokens, departments, and positions.
- Attendance core: Tamper-resistant check-in and check-out, shift scheduling, auto-checkout grace periods, dispute corrections, and audit history.
- Leave workflow: Entitlement balance tracking, concurrent reservation locking, manager approvals, medical certificate attachments, and cancellation compensations.
- Material and general requests: Multi-step approval workflows, advisory inventory checks, and private attachment downloads with short-lived tokens.
- Outbox and notifications: Database-backed Transactional Outbox, at-least-once local event dispatch, consumer idempotency receipts, and in-app user notifications.
- Audit and CSV reporting: Tamper-evident audit logging of all mutations, attendance roll-ups, leave utilization matrices, and streaming CSV exports.
- Client interfaces: Modern React web dashboard with TypeScript and a lightweight Flutter mobile client for daily employee attendance and request tracking.
- Operational infrastructure: Single-host Docker Compose deployment, PostgreSQL 16 domain schemas, Caddy reverse proxy, Cloudflare Tunnel ingress, and verified nightly backup scripts.

## Authoritative specifications

To avoid conflicting requirements, documentation follows the hierarchy established in the [Source of truth map](SOURCE-OF-TRUTH.md):

- [Architecture](Architecture.md): Authoritative definition of the modular monolith runtime, domain package boundaries, database schema boundaries, and security model.
- [API and persistence mapping](REST-API-DATABASE-DESIGN.md): Authoritative contract rules, REST route patterns, idempotency keys, outbox schema, and status code standards.
- [Decision register](roadmap/DECISION-REGISTER.md): Authoritative record of architectural choices, scope boundaries, and accepted operational trade-offs.
- [Architecture decision records](adr/README.md): ADR 001 through 006 providing formal context, options considered, and superseding rationale.
- [Reference index](reference/README.md): Historical reference material detailing earlier seven-service microservice and Kafka contracts, retained for historical background.

## Getting started as a new developer

New contributors must follow this reading and setup sequence to understand the project and prepare a working development environment:

1. Read this documentation handbook in full to understand the project goals, user roles, and system boundaries.
1. Inspect the [Source of truth map](SOURCE-OF-TRUTH.md) to understand which documents are normative.
1. Review [Start here](roadmap/START-HERE.md) for the daily 5-minute implementation routine and operational boundaries.
1. Inspect [You are here](roadmap/YOU-ARE-HERE.md) to determine the current implementation step, last verified milestone, and active blockers.
1. Review the [Project baseline](roadmap/00-PREPARATION/PROJECT-BASELINE.md) and [Repository audit](roadmap/00-PREPARATION/REPOSITORY-AUDIT.md) to understand the starting codebase state.

## Implementation roadmap structure

The engineering journey is organized into twelve sequential weekly phases, taking the project from initial repository preparation to production release:

| Week | Phase | Primary deliverable | Gate criteria |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 00 | [Preparation](roadmap/00-PREPARATION/README.md) | Baseline audit, hardware assessment, and migration strategy | Disk and toolchain gates verified |
| 01 | [Foundation](roadmap/01-FOUNDATION/README.md) | Walking skeleton, single-service boot, Docker Compose, and mock Flutter | Private web-to-app-to-DB ping **PASS** |
| 02 | [Identity and host](roadmap/02-IDENTITY-AND-HOST/README.md) | Multi-tenant auth, JWT refresh rotation, private host deployment | Two-tenant auth and deploy **PASS** |
| 03 | [Organization and admin](roadmap/03-ORGANIZATION-AND-ADMIN/README.md) | Org units, positions, employee profiles, and builder pattern lesson | Employee hierarchy tests **PASS** |
| 04 | [Attendance core](roadmap/04-ATTENDANCE-CORE/README.md) | Append-only evidence, shift windows, auto-checkout, corrections | Attendance invariant tests **PASS** |
| 05 | [Outbox and notifications](roadmap/05-OUTBOX-AND-NOTIFICATIONS/README.md) | Transactional outbox, inbox deduplication receipts, in-app notifications | At-least-once outbox test **PASS** |
| 06 | [Leave workflow](roadmap/06-LEAVE-WORKFLOW/README.md) | Entitlement balances, pessimistic reservation locks, manager approvals | Concurrency overspend test **PASS** |
| 07 | [Requests and approvals](roadmap/07-REQUESTS-AND-APPROVALS/README.md) | Material requests, private signed attachments, specification pattern | Attachment auth security **PASS** |
| 08 | [Web and mobile integration](roadmap/08-WEB-AND-MOBILE-INTEGRATION/README.md) | React frontend forms, live Flutter integration, offline command queue | End-to-end user journeys **PASS** |
| 09 | [Reporting and audit](roadmap/09-REPORTING-AUDIT-OBSERVABILITY/README.md) | Tamper-evident audit logs, CSV exports, Prometheus metrics, Uptime Kuma | Streaming export and health **PASS** |
| 10 | [Operations and restore](roadmap/10-OPERATIONS-AND-RESTORE/README.md) | Automated pg_dump, off-site disk replication, scratch disaster recovery | Clean-host disaster restore **PASS** |
| 11 | [Hardening and pilot](roadmap/11-HARDENING-AND-PILOT/README.md) | Security vulnerability scan, rate limiting, measured load testing | 50 concurrent virtual users **PASS** |
| 12 | [Release and demonstration](roadmap/12-RELEASE-AND-DEMONSTRATION/README.md) | Code freeze, user acceptance testing, operator training, release handoff | Stakeholder demonstration **PASS** |

## Build and test execution

The development environment requires Java 21, Maven 3.9+, Docker Desktop or Docker Engine, Node.js 20+, and Flutter 3.19+:

```bash
# Verify build environment prerequisites
java -version
docker compose -f infra/docker/docker-compose.yaml config --quiet
mvn -o validate
```

```bash
# Execute documentation suite linting
python3 docs/roadmap/tools/docs-lint.py docs
```

```bash
# Run unit and slice tests
mvn test
```

## Deployment, backup, and disaster recovery

HRFlow runs as a single self-contained application stack on a dedicated host machine:

- Runbook instructions: Detailed operational commands are documented in [Host runbook](roadmap/10-OPERATIONS-AND-RESTORE/HOST-RUNBOOK.md) and [Access setup](roadmap/02-IDENTITY-AND-HOST/ACCESS-SETUP.md).
- Automated backup: A scheduled nightly cron job executes `pg_dump` with custom compressed format, retaining 14 days of encrypted rolling snapshots.
- Off-site replication: Backup archives and uploaded private attachments are mirrored to an external physical storage disk disconnected from network exposure.
- Disaster recovery: A weekly scratch restore script recreates the database on an isolated temporary cluster, validating database integrity constraints and data recoverability.

## Risks, open decisions, and project tracking

Project health, risks, and progress are continuously tracked across central dashboards:

- [Risk register](roadmap/RISK-REGISTER.md): Active inventory of technical, operational, and schedule risks with documented mitigations.
- [Decision register](roadmap/DECISION-REGISTER.md): Record of all accepted architectural decisions and scope cut criteria.
- [Global checklist](roadmap/GLOBAL-CHECKLIST.md): Complete requirements coverage map connecting functional goals to verified tests.
- [Roadmap progress](roadmap/PROGRESS.md): Historical ledger of documentation phases, tool validations, and dry-run corrections.
- [Open questions](SOURCE-OF-TRUTH.md): Central register of outstanding decisions (O01 through O08) requiring stakeholder alignment.

# HRFlow twelve-week execution plan

> **Decision:** ADR 006 establishes the single Spring Boot modular monolith execution plan, superseding the seven-service roadmap. The target duration is twelve weeks (84 calendar days).

## Execution philosophy and delivery cadence

The execution plan prioritizes visible mini-wins, verifiable evidence, and strict capacity boundaries. Development follows a predictable weekly cadence designed to prevent burnout and ensure steady progress:

- Monday through Wednesday: Active feature development across Stones 1, 2, and 3. Each day contains three small, bounded steps (30 to 90 minutes each), introducing at most two new concepts per day.
- Thursday: Review, buffer, and failure recovery in Stone 4. Zero new feature scope is introduced; time is dedicated to test hardening, diagnostic reviews, and refactoring admitted patterns.
- Friday: Weekly gate execution, host redeployment, and disaster recovery testing in Stone 5. Critical gates must be verified on confirmed host infrastructure.
- Saturday and Sunday: Mandatory rest days. Crunch time and weekend work are prohibited; unfinished non-critical tasks are simplified or carried over.

## Capacity model and contributor allocation

Capacity planning accounts for real-world constraints, learning curves, and unexpected blockers:

| Metric | Contributor A (Backend/Infra/Web) | Contributor B (Mobile/QA/Client) | Combined team capacity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stated weekly commitment | 24.0 hours | 24.0 hours | 48.0 hours |
| Planned allocation (70%) | 16.8 hours | 16.8 hours | 33.6 hours |
| Light weeks allocation (Weeks 4 and 8) | 14.28 hours | 14.28 hours | 28.56 hours |
| Total planned twelve-week capacity | 196.56 hours | 196.56 hours | 393.12 hours |
| Core step implementation budget | 98.75 hours | 98.75 hours | 197.5 hours |
| Technical reading and primers budget | 24.0 hours | 24.0 hours | 48.0 hours |
| Buffer, recovery, and retro reserve | 73.81 hours | 73.81 hours | 147.62 hours |

## Twelve-week milestone roadmap

The implementation is partitioned into twelve sequential milestone weeks, each producing an independently testable increment:

| Week | Phase name | Key deliverables | Primary acceptance gate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | [Foundation](roadmap/01-FOUNDATION/README.md) | Single Boot app, PostgreSQL schemas, Caddy gateway, mock Flutter shell. | Web-to-Caddy-to-app-to-DB ping **PASS**. |
| 02 | [Identity and host](roadmap/02-IDENTITY-AND-HOST/README.md) | JWT access, rotating refresh tokens, private host deployment, initial dump. | Two-tenant auth and local deploy **PASS**. |
| 03 | [Organization and admin](roadmap/03-ORGANIZATION-AND-ADMIN/README.md) | Tenant onboarding, org units, positions, employee hierarchy, Builder pattern. | Org tree and employee assignment **PASS**. |
| 04 | [Attendance core](roadmap/04-ATTENDANCE-CORE/README.md) | Append-only evidence, shift windows, auto-checkout, manual corrections. | Attendance invariant test matrix **PASS**. |
| 05 | [Outbox and notifications](roadmap/05-OUTBOX-AND-NOTIFICATIONS/README.md) | Transactional outbox, inbox receipts, in-app notification inbox. | At-least-once outbox dispatch **PASS**. |
| 06 | [Leave workflow](roadmap/06-LEAVE-WORKFLOW/README.md) | Entitlement balances, pessimistic reservation locks, manager approvals. | Concurrency overspend test **PASS**. |
| 07 | [Requests and approvals](roadmap/07-REQUESTS-AND-APPROVALS/README.md) | Material requests, multi-level approvals, private attachment downloads. | Attachment auth and download **PASS**. |
| 08 | [Web and mobile integration](roadmap/08-WEB-AND-MOBILE-INTEGRATION/README.md) | React frontend dashboard, live Flutter integration, offline command queue. | End-to-end client user flows **PASS**. |
| 09 | [Reporting and audit](roadmap/09-REPORTING-AUDIT-OBSERVABILITY/README.md) | Tamper-evident audit logs, attendance summaries, CSV exports, Uptime Kuma. | Streaming CSV and health checks **PASS**. |
| 10 | [Operations and restore](roadmap/10-OPERATIONS-AND-RESTORE/README.md) | Automated pg_dump cron, off-site disk replication, clean-machine restore. | Full bare-metal disaster recovery **PASS**. |
| 11 | [Hardening and pilot](roadmap/11-HARDENING-AND-PILOT/README.md) | OWASP security review, rate limiting, measured load testing (50 users). | 50 concurrent virtual users **PASS**. |
| 12 | [Release and demonstration](roadmap/12-RELEASE-AND-DEMONSTRATION/README.md) | Code freeze, user acceptance testing, operator training, final handoff. | Stakeholder acceptance sign-off **PASS**. |

## Scope management and tiered features

Features are categorized into strict priority tiers to prevent deadline overruns:

- Tier 1 (Must-Have): Multi-tenant authentication, tenant isolation, organization hierarchy, attendance check-in/out, attendance corrections, leave balances with concurrency locks, material requests, private attachments, transactional outbox, in-app notifications, audit logs, basic CSV exports, React web UI, Flutter mobile client, Docker Compose deployment, automated backups, and verified scratch restore.
- Tier 2 (Should-Have): Mobile push notifications via APNs/FCM, Server-Sent Events (SSE) for live notification delivery, Wi-Fi network nudges, simple leave rule inference, Khmer language localization, advanced CSV filters.
- Tier 3 (Deferred / Out-of-Scope): Apache Kafka broker runtime, production ML model scoring, facial recognition biometrics, NFC hardware readers, continuous GPS tracking, Kubernetes manifests, Terraform cloud automation, distributed tracing (Zipkin/Jaeger), payroll processing, recruiting pipelines.

## Failure remediation and stop rules

When tasks encounter technical blockers or exceed time limits, developers must follow standard recovery rules:

- 45-minute rule: If a task makes zero observable progress for 45 minutes, stop coding immediately and consult [Troubleshooting](roadmap/01-FOUNDATION/TROUBLESHOOTING.md) and [Stuck protocol](roadmap/STUCK-PROTOCOL.md).
- 90-minute cut rule: If a task remains blocked after 90 minutes, apply the documented stone cut in the phase README. Never compromise tenant isolation or backup verification.
- Critical gate failures: If a Friday gate fails, record **FAIL** with safe reproduction output. The failed check carries over into Monday of the next week as Stone 1, cutting optional stretch scope.
- Git checkpointing: Every 30–90 minute step concludes with an atomic Git commit matching the prescribed message format. Stones conclude with a verified green tag (e.g., `w01-s03-green`).

# ADR-002: Tenant and persistence isolation

- Status: Proposed
- Date: 2026-10-22
- Decision owners: contributor A and contributor B; product/HR, security, and operator review where applicable.

## Supersession

[Current ADR](006-FINISH-LINE-MODULAR-MONOLITH.md) supersedes any old seven-service/Kafka/cloud assumptions; other proposals require current review.

## Context

Bootstrap SQL creates six schemas on one PostgreSQL instance; attendance selects its schema but shares local hrflow credentials. The old API draft expects tenant-owned records. No migrations or tenant authorization exist.

## Problem

Schema names and tenant_id columns alone do not prevent cross-service or cross-tenant access.

## Decision

Use service-owned schemas with distinct runtime roles and separate migration privileges. Derive tenant from verified token/event/job. Use tenant-scoped queries, composite keys/FKs, resource checks, scoped files/caches/exports. Evaluate RLS only as additional defense with transaction-local context and pool tests. Canonical identity schema is identity_org.

## Alternatives Considered

Database per service improves physical separation but increases cost; database per tenant increases migrations/operations; application-only tenant predicates are simpler but provide fewer database safeguards.

## Consequences

One physical instance keeps MVP cost manageable but shares capacity/outage risk. Composite constraints add verbosity and require consistent repository design. RLS remains optional pending tested operational support.

## Security and Operational Implications

Fail closed on unknown/stale authorization projections. Do not grant runtime roles schema-owner/superuser privileges. Tenant-controlled paths/headers never establish trust.

## Implementation and Migration

Introduce owner migrations/grants before business tables. Backfill and validate tenant associations before enabling stricter constraints on existing data. Test IDs/counts/SSE/files/jobs from a second tenant. This ADR is not approval of an implemented RLS policy.

## References

- [Detailed specification](../REST-API-DATABASE-DESIGN.md).
- [Execution plan](../PLAN.md).

# Architecture decision records

> **Decision:** ADR 006 is the authoritative active decision governing the HRFlow architecture. ADRs 001 through 005 document the design evolution from the initial microservice proposals to the accepted modular monolith.

## Architecture decision register

The following formal records document significant technical decisions, structural trade-offs, and operational boundaries:

| ID | Title | Status | Date | Primary scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [001](001-SERVICE-AND-EVENT-BOUNDARIES.md) | Service and event boundaries | Superseded | 2026-10-22 | Initial seven-service microservices and Kafka proposal; superseded by ADR 006. |
| [002](002-TENANT-AND-PERSISTENCE-ISOLATION.md) | Tenant and persistence isolation | Accepted | 2026-10-22 | Strict database schema boundaries, composite tenant keys, and token-derived tenancy. |
| [003](003-EVENT-DELIVERY-AND-CONTRACTS.md) | Event delivery and contracts | Refined | 2026-10-22 | Transactional outbox and consumer inbox receipts; runtime broker deferred by ADR 006. |
| [004](004-ATTENDANCE-AND-LEAVE-CONFLICTS.md) | Attendance and leave conflicts | Accepted | 2026-10-22 | Precedence rules, manual correction precedence, and human review states. |
| [005](005-DEPLOYMENT-AND-CLIENT-BASELINE.md) | Deployment and client baseline | Superseded | 2026-10-22 | Initial proposal to retain Nuxt and explore Kubernetes; superseded by ADR 006. |
| [006](006-FINISH-LINE-MODULAR-MONOLITH.md) | Finish-line modular monolith | Accepted | 2026-10-23 | Authoritative baseline: single Spring Boot app, domain schemas, React, Caddy, and Tunnel. |

## Supersession and dependency matrix

Understanding the relationship between historical and active decisions ensures consistent implementation:

- Service topology: ADR 001 proposed seven microservices connected via Kafka. ADR 006 supersedes this topology, consolidating services into domain packages (`identityorg`, `attendance`, `leave`, `request`, `notification`, `reporting`) within one Spring Boot modular monolith in `services/hrflow-app`.
- Persistence boundaries: ADR 002 established schema-level isolation. ADR 006 preserves this rule: six separate PostgreSQL schemas within a single shared database instance, forbidding cross-schema foreign keys and queries.
- Asynchronous messaging: ADR 003 established the Transactional Outbox pattern. ADR 006 refines this pattern by utilizing local database tables (`notification.outbox_events` and `notification.inbox_receipts`) polled by an in-process worker, deferring Kafka runtime dependencies.
- Business conflicts: ADR 004 established attendance and leave reconciliation rules. ADR 006 adopts these domain invariants without modification.
- Frontend and hosting: ADR 005 considered retaining Nuxt and deploying to Kubernetes. ADR 006 supersedes ADR 005, mandating React with TypeScript for web, Flutter for mobile, and Docker Compose with Cloudflare Tunnel for self-hosting.

## Reading and lifecycle guidelines

When evaluating technical architecture or proposing modifications:

- Implementation guides must conform to active ADRs: An implementation guide or pull request cannot violate an accepted ADR without submitting a new superseding decision record.
- Historical context: Superseded ADRs are preserved to explain why specific alternatives were rejected and under what conditions they may be reconsidered.
- Canonical references: Cross-reference architectural specifications in [Architecture](../Architecture.md) and operational trade-offs in [Decision register](../roadmap/DECISION-REGISTER.md).

# ADR-001: Service and event boundaries

- Status: Superseded
- Date: 2026-10-22
- Decision owners: contributor A and contributor B; product/HR, security, and operator review where applicable.

## Supersession

[Current ADR](006-FINISH-LINE-MODULAR-MONOLITH.md) supersedes any old seven-service/Kafka/cloud assumptions; other proposals require current review.

## Context

The pre-existing Plan.md explicitly defines seven domain services, gateway-only client entry, Kafka-only business integration, local read models, and no cross-service joins. Source contains matching service scaffolds but not business implementations.

## Problem

Preserve domain ownership while avoiding synchronous business dependencies and an unrealistic all-services-first delivery strategy.

## Decision

Retain api-gateway, identity-org, attendance, leave, request, notification, reporting as logical boundaries. Clients call gateway; services integrate business facts through Kafka. No cross-service SQL/foreign keys or business HTTP. Acceptance refers only to the pre-existing intended baseline, not working deployment. A proposed security-control-plane exception permits cached JWKS discovery. Build one end-to-end slice first; merging reporting/notification projections remains an existing documented contingency.

## Alternatives Considered

A modular monolith reduces operations but changes the established baseline; independent services with HTTP simplify reads but couple availability; a service mesh adds unjustified MVP complexity.

## Consequences

Local reads keep check-in independent of remote latency. Eventual consistency, snapshot evolution, reconciliation, and additional deployments are real costs. Boundary changes require new evidence and ADR rather than directory renames.

## Security and Operational Implications

Gateway auth does not replace service authorization. Topic ownership, private listeners, and tenant scope must be enforced. A shared DB/broker still creates shared failure domains.

## Implementation and Migration

Implement identity/attendance/event foundation before expanding other workflows. Record and test any communication exception. No HTTP business fallback during projection lag.

## References

- [Detailed specification](../Architecture.md).
- [Execution plan](../PLAN.md).

# ADR-005: Deployment and client baseline

- Status: Superseded
- Date: 2026-10-22
- Decision owners: contributor A and contributor B; product/HR, security, and operator review where applicable.

## Supersession

[Current ADR](006-FINISH-LINE-MODULAR-MONOLITH.md) supersedes any old seven-service/Kafka/cloud assumptions; other proposals require current review.

## Context

The old plan specifies React and eventual EKS/k3s, while source is Nuxt/Vue and dependency-only Compose. No cloud/cluster/IaC/CI resources exist. One contributor owns backend/web/infrastructure and the budget alert is `$30`, not a cost forecast.

## Problem

Framework rewrite and premature Kubernetes can consume the twelve-week delivery without improving core correctness.

## Decision

Propose retaining Nuxt for MVP and using a simple reproducible container pilot deployment before Kubernetes. Keep Flutter as intended mobile client. O01 selects frontend and O04 selects hosting/cost/operations. EKS is optional future infrastructure, not a release requirement. No dependency changes are authorized by this ADR.

## Alternatives Considered

React aligns with original UI plan but requires replacing scaffold; k3s provides Kubernetes with self-managed operations; EKS supplies managed control plane but adds cost and networking complexity; a single host is simpler but not highly available.

## Consequences

Preserves implementation momentum with explicit limitations. Production launch still needs TLS, secrets, backups, restore/rollback, private stores, and an operator. Deployment simplicity does not waive security.

## Security and Operational Implications

Single-host/broker failures are expected pilot outage risks. Forecast cloud spend before provisioning; budget alert does not cap spend. Keep database/Kafka/Registry private.

## Implementation and Migration

Complete local startup, CI/images, and staged smoke first. Record final target and accepted risk before real users. If React is selected, migrate before feature UI work; API contracts remain independent of framework.

## References

- [Detailed specification](../Architecture.md).
- [Execution plan](../PLAN.md).

# ADR-004: Attendance and leave conflicts

- Status: Proposed
- Date: 2026-10-22
- Decision owners: contributor A and contributor B; product/HR, security, and operator review where applicable.

## Supersession

[Current ADR](006-FINISH-LINE-MODULAR-MONOLITH.md) supersedes any old seven-service/Kafka/cloud assumptions; other proposals require current review.

## Context

The plan says Holiday > Approved leave > Manual > Inferred > Absent and also manual records always win. The old API supports multiple sessions and append-only corrections. The leave saga moves approval conflicts to NEEDS_REVIEW but does not define balances/compensation.

## Problem

A single precedence enum can discard evidence or hide work on leave/holiday. Automatic compensation can refund leave incorrectly.

## Decision

Separate calendar day type, effective session evidence, attendance flags, and review state. Manual approved interpretation supersedes inferred interpretation without deleting evidence. Overlapping approved leave/manual work produces a review conflict. Proposed NEEDS_REVIEW retains debit/overlay until HR explicitly keeps or cancels leave; cancellation creates compensating ledger and newer snapshot. O02 approval is required before automatic resolution; overnight and inference windows remain O03.

## Alternatives Considered

Calendar-always-wins hides observed work; manual-always-wins silently invalidates approved leave; immediate automatic refund risks wrong balances; explicit conflict review costs human effort but preserves facts.

## Consequences

More expressive day response and visible exceptions are needed. Reports use current daily revision, not raw session count. Legacy enum alone is insufficient when late and early both apply.

## Security and Operational Implications

Only authorized independent approvers resolve conflicts/corrections. Record reasons, actor, request approval revision, session references, and decision history. Do not use evidence confidence as disciplinary proof.

## Implementation and Migration

Implement conflict-free same-day check-in first. Block silent overlap finalization until policy approval. Use request revision guards so delayed conflict cannot resurrect cancelled leave; test duplicate compensation and late evidence.

## References

- [Detailed specification](../Architecture.md).
- [Execution plan](../PLAN.md).

# ADR 006 — Finish-line modular monolith

## Status and owners

Status: Accepted for the build guide by the explicit 2026-10-23 user instructions and the default consolidation rule for mostly unbuilt code. Owners: A and B; HR/privacy/host readiness still require the named external input. Supersedes ADR 001 deployment/communication baseline and ADR 005 client/hosting proposals. No claim that code has migrated.

## Context and problem

Seven services contain only startup scaffolds, source is Nuxt, current host has about 5 GiB free, and no deployed system exists. A junior team cannot justify seven deployment/broker boundaries from existing behavior. User explicitly requires React, existing-host Compose, safe HTTPS, nightly external backups and a twelve-week deadline.

## Decision

- **Decision:** Outcome C, one Boot app with domain packages and owner schemas; local transactional outbox/receipts for notification/reporting; React and early mocked Flutter.
- **Reason:** Counted step ledger is 197.5 core contributor-hours plus reading/buffer within provisional 393.12 planned hours at interpreted 24 h each. More deployables add unproven operational work.
- **Rejected alternatives:** Seven microservices, separate worker runtime, Kubernetes/Terraform/cloud infrastructure, Kafka runtime without two truly independent async components.
- **Implementation impact:** Migration is incremental on code branches, old source preserved; routes and tenant/domain correctness remain. OpenAPI is one wire source; package APIs/projections enforce ownership.
- **Cost and operational impact:** One host/DB remains a shared failure domain. Tunnel is free publishing plus domain cost, not free hardware/power/ISP or high availability. External backup media is required.
- **Reconsider when:** Measured independent deployment/load need and a tested capacity/operations budget justify extracting a component.

## Security and operational implications

Token-derived tenant, object checks, scoped constraints, HTTPS/auth/firewall/secrets/verified backup before exposure remain mandatory. Cloudflare public TLS and private Caddy origin are chosen because WAN capability is unknown. Nightly custom dump and external copy plus scratch/clean-host restores protect data; provider/ISP/power outage still stops remote availability.

## Implementation and migration

[Migration plan](../roadmap/00-PREPARATION/MIGRATION-PLAN.md) names the inspected current files and proposed target paths. Java 21/Boot 4.1.1 existing root baseline remains; no app dependencies changed by documentation. Kafka-specific tests are not falsely claimed for local receipts. Future Kafka reintroduction requires new ADR and real broker crash/offset tests.

## Consequences

Development gets fewer operational boundaries, while data/package discipline requires explicit tests. Estimated capacity remains conditional on actual hours and junior velocity. Unknown host/domain/disk/start date are blockers, not blank completed tasks. No pattern quota overrides current need.

## References

- [Architecture](../Architecture.md).

# ADR-003: Event delivery and contracts

- Status: Proposed
- Date: 2026-10-22
- Decision owners: contributor A and contributor B; product/HR, security, and operator review where applicable.

## Supersession

[Current ADR](006-FINISH-LINE-MODULAR-MONOLITH.md) supersedes any old seven-service/Kafka/cloud assumptions; other proposals require current review.

## Context

The existing plan requires outbox/inbox and versioned events. The repository has one flat Avro check-in record, a partially configured Registry, and no relay/consumer implementation. JSON Schema/AsyncAPI in the old plan conflicts with Avro source.

## Problem

Need durable publication, safe duplicate/order handling, and one explicit contract strategy without claiming distributed exactly-once behavior.

## Decision

Implement atomic business+outbox writes, lease-based ordered aggregate-head relay, stable event IDs, local inbox+effect transactions, and Kafka acknowledgment only after commit. Snapshots guard aggregateVersion. Proposed normalized envelope and catalog are authoritative design; serialization choice O06 remains open. Prefer completing existing Avro path only if its operational cost/compatibility tests are accepted; otherwise choose JSON explicitly before publishing.

## Alternatives Considered

Direct DB+Kafka dual-write can lose/phantom facts; Kafka transactions do not atomically commit PostgreSQL; CDC/Debezium reduces custom relay work but adds operations; in-memory deduplication fails across restart.

## Consequences

At-least-once delivery is expected. Duplicate publication after crash is harmless only with tested consumer/domain safeguards. SKIP LOCKED does not guarantee aggregate order without head eligibility. Replay retention and compaction need intentional keys.

## Security and Operational Implications

Restrict producers by topic ACL; protect DLQ payloads. Never replay live provider notifications during projection rebuild. Monitor age/backlog, not only broker process health.

## Implementation and Migration

Correct Avro generation path and Registry connectivity if retained. Do not mutate legacy flat schema in place into an incompatible envelope. Add contract fixtures/compatibility checks and a controlled transition before first real producer.

## References

- [Detailed specification](../Architecture.md).
- [Execution plan](../PLAN.md).

# Git safety

## Before changes

This repo began without commits and with staged source plus untracked work. Never run a blanket add/commit before reviewing secrets and generated folders. During the guide create a private safe initial code commit, then weekly branches such as `build/week-01`. Documentation is on `docs/roadmap-playbook`.

```bash
git status --short
git diff
git diff --cached
```

Inspect intended paths, secrets, and test output before staging explicitly. A commit is a checkpoint, not proof that a feature works.

## Step and stone checkpoints

Every step ends with a focused commit such as `feat(attendance): validate checkout interval`. Every stone ends with a lightweight tag matching its final step, for example `w04-s03-green`. Tests must pass and app startup must be demonstrated before tagging. Never create these tags while merely writing the guide.

```bash
git add PATH_REVIEWED_BY_YOU
git commit -m 'feat(attendance): validate checkout interval'
git tag w04-s03-green
git show --stat w04-s03-green
```

`PATH_REVIEWED_BY_YOU` is a token to replace with a real reviewed path, not a literal command argument to copy blindly.

## Return to green without deleting work

First commit a safe work-in-progress on the current branch, or stash only reviewed non-secret paths. Never stash secrets expecting a security boundary. Then create a recovery branch from the verified tag; old branch and commits remain available.

```bash
git status --short
git stash push -u -m 'safe reviewed work before recovery' -- REVIEWED_PATH
git stash list
git switch -c recovery/week-04 w04-s03-green
```

Inspect `git stash show --stat` before using `git stash apply`; prefer apply over pop so the backup remains until verified. Resolve conflicts in a separate commit; do not force the tag to move. Restore database from scratch backup only in a scratch instance until explicit production recovery approval.

## Commands never to use as routine recovery

Do not run `git reset --hard`, `git clean -fd`, force push, history rewriting, `docker compose down -v`, or `docker system prune`. They can destroy work or data. Do not revert unrelated user changes. Database rollback is not the same as changing a Git branch; use additive migrations and verified restore procedures.

# Stuck protocol

## Forty-five minute boundary

1. Stop editing. Write the current step ID and last observed result.
1. Re-read Why, Before you start, and Expect; confirm you are not running a future command.
1. Run the current week's diagnostic in TROUBLESHOOTING.md and capture safe output.
1. Build the smallest reproduction: one request, one employee, one transaction, one failing test.
1. Write the question below; ask the other contributor or mentor with the reproduction.

## Question template

- Did: exact step and command, with secrets removed.
- Expected: the guide's exact response/test/row count.
- Happened: actual code/message and reproducible conditions.
- Tried: each attempted change and its result, including what was reverted safely.
- Last green: tag and database migration state.
- Needed: one concrete answer, not a screenshot of an entire desktop.

## Ninety-minute boundary

Apply the stone's skip-or-simplify rule from the weekly README. Cut stretch only. A critical authentication, attendance, leave concurrency, event durability, deploy, or restore failure is **FAIL** and moves into next week's first stone. Record owner and next action; do not label it passed to maintain the schedule.

## Shut down safely

- [ ] Commit reviewed safe work or keep it on an explicit WIP branch.
- [ ] Put the next small diagnostic in the dashboard.
- [ ] Preserve test evidence and last green tag.
- [ ] Stop for the day if tired; buffer time is planned work, not failure.

# Developer onboarding and daily execution guide

> **Navigation:** [Documentation root](../README.md) · [Source of truth](../SOURCE-OF-TRUTH.md) · [Current dashboard](YOU-ARE-HERE.md) · [Roadmap](ROADMAP.md)

## Ten-minute orientation

Welcome to the HRFlow engineering roadmap. This documentation is an executable, build-along playbook designed to guide developers from an unbuilt scaffolding repository to a fully tested, production-ready modular monolith.

Crucial operational realities to understand before writing code:

- Work is unbuilt: Scaffolding exists in `services/` and `web/`, but core HR business features are planned, not implemented.
- Evidence-based status: Implementation steps are marked **Not run** until you execute the step, run its verification tests, and record authentic test outputs.
- Proposed paths: Commands referencing files that do not exist yet (such as `services/hrflow-app` or `contracts/openapi.yaml`) indicate targets to create during that designated step.

## The five daily files

Every developer must keep these five central files bookmarked during daily implementation:

1. [You are here](YOU-ARE-HERE.md): Your primary active dashboard indicating the current week, next step ID, last verified green milestone tag, and active blockers.
1. [Current build guide](01-FOUNDATION/BUILD-GUIDE.md): The step-by-step manual for the active week, specifying exact prerequisites, implementation tasks, and test commands.
1. [Current gate](01-FOUNDATION/VERIFY-AND-GATE.md): The acceptance test matrix, regression checks, and exit criteria required before closing the week.
1. [Stuck protocol](STUCK-PROTOCOL.md): The time-boxed 45-minute and 90-minute escalation procedures for recovering from unexpected blockers.
1. [Global checklist](GLOBAL-CHECKLIST.md): The complete functional requirements traceability matrix mapping business features to verified test evidence.

## The daily five-minute routine

To ensure continuous, sustainable velocity and avoid fatigue, follow this three-phase daily routine:

- Morning kickoff (2 minutes): Open [You are here](YOU-ARE-HERE.md) to inspect today's assigned step. Check prerequisites in the active build guide. Confirm that you have energy (rested, steady, or tired) and start a 45-minute timer before writing code.
- Focused execution (30 to 90 minutes): Work on one single, bounded implementation step. Introduce no more than two new concepts per day. Run the step's specific check command.
- Evening shutdown (3 minutes): Commit only intended files with a conventional commit message. If completing a stepping stone, tag the commit. Record safe output evidence in the dashboard, update tomorrow's first step, and close your laptop.

## Weekly cadence and operational boundaries

The twelve-week curriculum enforces strict weekly boundaries to guarantee code quality and prevent burnout:

- Monday through Wednesday: Active implementation across Stones 1, 2, and 3 (three 30–90 minute steps per day).
- Thursday: Review and buffer in Stone 4. Zero new feature scope may be introduced. Time is dedicated to test hardening, diagnostic investigations, and refactoring admitted patterns.
- Friday: Stone 5 gate execution, private host deployment, and automated scratch disaster recovery testing.
- Saturday and Sunday: Mandatory rest days. Never pay for missed weekday tasks with weekend work.

## Escalation and stop rules

If an implementation step encounters technical difficulties:

- 45-minute limit: If you make zero observable progress for 45 minutes, stop coding and consult the active week's `TROUBLESHOOTING.md` and [Stuck protocol](STUCK-PROTOCOL.md).
- 90-minute cut rule: If a task remains blocked after 90 minutes, apply the documented stone cut in the phase README. Never skip multi-tenant security or backup verification.
- Critical gate failures: If a Friday gate fails, record **FAIL**. The failed check becomes Monday's first action in the following week, cutting non-essential stretch features.

# HRFlow glossary

## Terms used by the guide

**Tenant:** An isolated company scope derived from a verified token.

**Principal:** Authenticated user/service identity, distinct from employee record.

**JWT:** Signed short-lived access token; decoding is not signature validation.

**Refresh family:** Related rotating refresh secrets, stored hashed and revoked on reuse.

**Migration:** Versioned database change applied once.

**Invariant:** A condition that must remain true under retries and concurrency.

**Idempotency:** Same command identity yields one intended effect.

**Outbox:** Durable event intent committed with domain data.

**Inbox:** Receipt committed with a handler effect to prevent duplicates.

**Projection:** Derived read model with source revision and visible freshness.

**Aggregate revision:** Monotonic owner state version, not wall-clock order.

**Lease:** Time-limited worker claim recoverable after a crash.

**CGNAT:** ISP translation that prevents ordinary inbound router forwarding.

**Reverse proxy:** Gateway forwarding approved requests to private application.

**TLS:** Encrypted authenticated network transport.

**RPO:** Maximum agreed data-loss interval, not a promise from a backup filename.

**RTO:** Agreed recovery duration measured by drills.

**Green tag:** Git label for tested app startup and a stone win.

**Mock server:** Responses generated from OpenAPI before live implementation.

**Testcontainers:** Real disposable dependency containers started by tests.

**CI:** Automated build/tests on pushes, with secrets protected.

**Cron:** Host scheduler; sleeping/unavailable host can miss jobs.

**Uptime Kuma:** Private availability monitoring; cannot alert externally when its entire host is down.

**Caddy:** Reverse proxy; public automatic TLS requires reachable validation or configured DNS.

**Cloudflare Tunnel:** Outbound connector; remote access still depends on ISP/provider.

# Decision register

## Architecture outcome C

- **Decision:** One Spring Boot application in proposed `services/hrflow-app`, packages `com.hrflow.app.identityorg`, `attendance`, `leave`, `request`, `notification`, and `reporting`; one Caddy edge gateway. No Kafka runtime for MVP.
- **Reason:** Seven services are startup scaffolds. The counted plan fits only provisional capacity with the fewest deployables.
- **Rejected alternatives:** Seven service deployments and a separately deployed worker add integration/operations work without existing behavior to preserve.
- **Implementation impact:** Preserve domain package/schema ownership, migrate endpoints without URL changes, keep PostgreSQL transactional outbox and per-handler inbox. Local workers replace Kafka delivery; no Kafka offsets exist on this path.
- **Cost and operational impact:** One app, PostgreSQL, Caddy, Uptime Kuma, and optional tunnel connector. No cloud database, Kubernetes, Terraform, Registry, or broker bill. Existing computer/power/domain/disk still cost money.
- **Reconsider when:** Two independently deployed components demonstrably need broker decoupling and a measured capacity budget supports migration.

[Capacity math](00-PREPARATION/PROJECT-BASELINE.md) and [migration](00-PREPARATION/MIGRATION-PLAN.md) are normative. The decision is settled for this guide; uncertain hours remain a feasibility assumption.

## Fixed choices

| Area | Choice | Implementation point | Gate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Java | Java 21 with existing root Boot 4.1.1 baseline | New app inherits reviewed parent; no framework upgrade | W1 compile |
| Web | React with TypeScript | Preserve Nuxt history, migrate deliberately | W1 thin view |
| Mobile | Flutter, repository location verified first | Mock generated from one OpenAPI file | W1 mock, W8 real integration |
| API | Proposed `contracts/openapi.yaml` sole wire authority | Preserve old domain routes, incremental implemented coverage | W1 validation |
| Persistence | PostgreSQL 16, schema per domain, Flyway | Never edit an applied migration | W1 and every deploy |
| Events | JSON outbox and transactional local handlers | Handler effects/inbox in DB transaction; external delivery separate | W5 recovery |
| Auth | JWT access, rotating hashed refresh families | Token tenant only; local admin provisioning separate | W2 negative tests |
| Host | Existing computer, Docker Compose | Private deployment in W2, weekly redeploy | W2 and W10 |
| Access | Cloudflare Tunnel to private Caddy origin | Unknown WAN/CGNAT; no port forwarding | External access blocked until safe |
| TLS | Automatic public TLS at Cloudflare edge | Caddy private origin not falsely advertised as ACME TLS | W2 verify chain |
| Backups | Nightly custom pg_dump, 14 days, external copy | Weekly scratch restore; no automatic production overwrite | W2 first restore |
| Monitoring | Actuator, Docker health/restart/log limits, Uptime Kuma | Private monitoring/admin only | W2 then W9 |
| Storage | Private host directory with metadata/backups | No S3 requirement; attachments capped and authorized | W7 |
| Notifications | Durable in-app inbox, local delivery adapter | Push should-have until provider/account/device proof | W5 |
| Patterns | Two admitted lessons, six conditional candidates | Baseline/pain before abstraction, no quota | Learning path |

## Scope tiers

- Must: auth/tenant and resource checks; org; attendance; leave/approval; material/special requests; in-app notifications; audit; basic CSV; React; Flutter; local outbox reliability; self-host deploy and tested restore.
- If stable: device push, SSE, geofence/Wi-Fi nudges, rule inference, EN/KH, extra reports, additional pattern refactors.
- Defer: ML, Kafka runtime, vision/camera, NFC, Redis, Kubernetes, Terraform, tracing stacks, dark mode, payroll, recruitment, continuous GPS, authoritative inventory.

## Product ambiguity decisions

Calendar and evidence are separate: holiday/leave never deletes work evidence. Manual approved corrections supersede inferred interpretations; overlap requires HR review. NEEDS_REVIEW retains leave debit until explicit HR cancellation or keep-leave resolution. Single same-day shift is MVP; reject unsupported overnight input. These are the guide's safe default policies, requiring HR approval before real data, not fabricated prior agreement.

## External dependencies

Cloudflare Tunnel free publishing requires domain/DNS control and relies on Cloudflare plus the ISP; there is no hosting SLA. Domain registrar price is unknown. Direct Caddy public TLS requires reachable 80/443 and is deferred unless new network evidence justifies an ADR change.

# Canonical Markdown formatting standard

> **Note:** This standard defines the cross-platform Markdown contract for all HRFlow technical documentation. It guarantees clean rendering across IntelliJ IDEA Markdown Preview, Notion import, and Obsidian Reading and Editing views without requiring proprietary plugins.

## Core principles

Every document in the HRFlow documentation suite must adhere to standard GitHub-Flavored Markdown. To ensure portability across diverse viewers, documents must avoid editor-specific extensions, custom HTML styling, and brittle syntax.

- Predictable layout: Every file follows a uniform structure with an explicit title, logical sections, and actionable next steps.
- Plain text portability: The documentation remains fully readable when viewed in raw text, terminal pagers, or code diffs.
- Automated verification: Format compliance is strictly enforced by the repository linter before any commit is accepted.
- Zero silent failures: Status indicators, test results, and gate criteria must use explicit bold status keywords.

## Heading hierarchy

Documents must maintain an unambiguous heading outline. Navigators and outline panes rely on consistent heading levels to build the document tree.

- Exactly one H1 title at the first line of the document.
- Use H2 for major structural sections.
- Use H3 for detailed subsections within an H2 section.
- Avoid H4 or deeper headings; restructure deeply nested content into separate focused documents.
- Never skip heading levels (e.g., jumping from H1 directly to H3).
- Headings must consist of plain text only. Do not place backticks, links, bold tags, or inline code inside headings.

## Paragraphs and text formatting

Prose explanations must prioritize clarity, density, and readability.

- Write one logical thought per line without hard-wrapped line breaks.
- Separate paragraphs with exactly one blank line.
- Use bold formatting selectively for key terminology, requirements, and status indicators.
- Avoid decorating entire sentences or paragraphs with bold or italic markers.
- Wrap inline variables, placeholders, file paths, and environment settings in backticks.
- Dollar signs (`$`) and hash marks (`#`) must be wrapped in backticks to prevent unwanted math or tag rendering.
- Raw HTML tags, line break tags, and custom font styling are strictly prohibited.

## Lists and actionable checklists

Lists structure non-sequential items, procedural workflows, and verification tasks.

- Unordered lists must use the hyphen marker (`-`).
- Ordered lists must use the number-dot marker (`1.`).
- Nested lists must use four spaces of indentation per level, capped at two levels of nesting.
- Always include a blank line before starting any list block.
- Checklists use the standard format `- [ ]` for incomplete tasks.
- Authored guides must leave checklist items unchecked (`- [ ]`); tasks are checked only during active execution.
- Checklists must never be placed inside table cells.

## Tables

Tables are reserved for structured comparisons, schema definitions, and concise status matrices.

- Limit tables to a maximum of six columns to prevent horizontal overflow in mobile and notebook screens.
- Every table must include a complete header row and a standard separator row (`| --- |`).
- Never leave table cells empty; use an em dash (`—`) when no value is applicable.
- Do not embed code blocks, multi-paragraph text, or task checkboxes inside table cells.
- Keep table cell text concise; link to referenced documents for extensive explanations.

## Code blocks and command conventions

Code examples and commands must provide complete, copy-pasteable context.

- Fenced code blocks must declare an explicit language identifier from the approved set: `java`, `sql`, `yaml`, `bash`, `json`, `ts`, `dart`, `xml`, `properties`, `text`, or `mermaid`.
- Individual lines within code blocks must not exceed 100 characters in width.
- Shell command blocks must omit shell prompts (`$` or `#`) to allow clean copying.
- Every command must clearly state its working directory, prerequisites, expected output, and failure remediation.
- Never place actual passwords, JWT secret keys, API tokens, or production hostnames in code examples.

## Callouts and blockquotes

Portable callouts use standard Markdown blockquotes with an approved bold prefix.

- Callouts must begin with one of the approved labels: `> **Note:**`, `> **Warning:**`, `> **Decision:**`, `> **Evidence:**`, `> **Pitfall:**`, or `> **Navigation:**`.
- Keep callout text focused on a single paragraph.
- Do not use Obsidian admonition syntax (such as `[!NOTE]`) or Notion custom callout blocks.

## Diagrams and visual models

Mermaid diagrams provide architectural and workflow visualizations without external binary assets.

- Supported diagram types are `flowchart`, `sequenceDiagram`, `erDiagram`, and `stateDiagram-v2`.
- Flowchart node labels must be enclosed in double quotes within brackets (e.g., `A["Client"]`).
- Limit diagrams to at most 15 nodes to maintain readability on standard screens.
- Custom node styling, CSS classes, and link styles are forbidden.
- Every Mermaid block must be immediately followed by a `Text version:` label and a bulleted list describing the flow.

## Links and cross-references

Navigation relies exclusively on relative Markdown links.

- Links must point directly to existing `.md` files using relative paths (e.g., `[Architecture](../Architecture.md)`).
- Anchor links (using `#`), folder-only links, and direct source code links are forbidden in portable documentation.
- Use descriptive link text that identifies the target document rather than generic phrases like "click here."

## Target platform verification

The documentation suite must be validated across the three primary viewing environments:

- IntelliJ IDEA: Open the built-in Markdown Preview. Verify heading outlines, table borders, syntax highlighting, and link traversal.
- Notion: Import Markdown documents via the standard page import. Confirm that tables, code fences, and blockquotes render cleanly without markdown syntax leakage.
- Obsidian: Open the `docs` folder as a dedicated vault. Ensure that reading view displays callouts, lists, and Mermaid diagrams correctly without requiring third-party plugins.

## Automated validation command

Run the repository linter before every commit to ensure zero formatting errors:

```bash
python3 docs/roadmap/tools/docs-lint.py docs
```

The script verifies file encoding, line endings, heading structure, table widths, code fences, Mermaid syntax, and relative link targets. All checks must pass with zero errors.

# Risk register

## Rating

Likelihood, impact and severity use High/Med/Low. High-impact correctness/data-loss issues remain critical even when likelihood is lower. These are planning judgments, not measured probabilities.

## Architecture complexity

- Likelihood: High; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Services/broker before first slice.
- Prevention: Choose one app and local outbox.
- Contingency: Park scaffold deployables, keep package boundaries.
- Owner: A; milestone: W1.

## Learning time

- Likelihood: High; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Step repeatedly exceeds 90 minutes.
- Prevention: Two concepts/day and primers.
- Contingency: Buffer and smaller reproduction, no weekend.
- Owner: A+B; milestone: Every gate.

## Burnout and overload

- Likelihood: High; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Tired shutdowns and missed rest.
- Prevention: 70 percent plan, two rest days, lighter W4/W8.
- Contingency: Cut stretch and stop sessions.
- Owner: A+B; milestone: W4/W8.

## Backend/mobile integration

- Likelihood: High; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Mock differs from live payload.
- Prevention: OpenAPI and B starts W1.
- Contingency: Fix one contract and both clients together.
- Owner: A+B; milestone: W8.

## Kafka reliability

- Likelihood: Med; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Someone adds broker without operational budget.
- Prevention: No Kafka runtime in outcome C.
- Contingency: Require new ADR and real-broker tests before adoption.
- Owner: A; milestone: W5/W10.

## API contract drift

- Likelihood: High; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Multiple schema files/DTO-only changes.
- Prevention: Single wire contract and CI fixture validation.
- Contingency: Freeze affected API and repair mocks/live tests.
- Owner: A+B; milestone: W8.

## Auth and tenant defects

- Likelihood: Med; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Scoped counts/object IDs leak.
- Prevention: Negative tests and scoped repository/constraints.
- Contingency: Block exposure; fix smallest tenant reproduction.
- Owner: A; milestone: W2/W11.

## Attendance defects

- Likelihood: High; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Grace/date/retry inconsistencies.
- Prevention: Fixed-clock interval and duplicate/race tests.

## Lost or duplicated events

- Likelihood: High; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Pending intents age or double inbox.
- Prevention: Atomic write and per-handler receipt.
- Contingency: Resume replay idempotently, preserve malformed intent.
- Owner: A; milestone: W5.

## Weak tests

- Likelihood: High; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Echo-only runner or mocked database.
- Prevention: Real PostgreSQL Testcontainers and assertions.
- Contingency: Gate stays **FAIL** until reproducible proof.
- Owner: A+B; milestone: Every gate.

## Limited hardware

- Likelihood: High; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Less than 30 GiB free or swapping.
- Prevention: Disk gate and narrow topology.
- Contingency: No pulls; get owner-approved storage headroom.
- Owner: A; milestone: W1/W2.

## ISP CGNAT dynamic IP

- Likelihood: High; impact: Med; severity: Med.
- Early warning: Remote timeout/router unavailable.
- Prevention: Outbound tunnel, inspect ISP privately.
- Contingency: Private host demo with external gate **FAIL**.
- Owner: A; milestone: W2.

## Power loss

- Likelihood: Med; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Machine sleeps or needs login.
- Prevention: Document awake/login behavior and backup age.
- Contingency: Restore/restart runbook and outage disclosure.
- Owner: A; milestone: W10.

## Single-host failure

- Likelihood: Med; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Hardware outage removes all components.
- Prevention: External backup and clean restore rehearsal.
- Contingency: Recover on replacement host, no HA claim.
- Owner: A; milestone: W10/W12.

## Disk exhaustion

- Likelihood: High; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Backup/export/log growth.
- Prevention: Log limits, retention, disk alerts.
- Contingency: Stop admission before false success; inspect without destructive prune.
- Owner: A; milestone: W10.

## Data loss

- Likelihood: Med; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Only copy is on same disk.
- Prevention: External verified backup.
- Contingency: Restore clean and reconcile business state.
- Owner: A+B; milestone: W10.

## Failed migrations

- Likelihood: Med; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Checksum mismatch or startup schema error.
- Prevention: Never edit applied SQL, expand-compatible change.
- Contingency: Forward fix or compatible image rollback.
- Owner: A; milestone: Every Friday.

## Untested backups

- Likelihood: High; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Cron success without restore.
- Prevention: Weekly scratch restore and age/checksum.
- Contingency: Do not expose externally, repair backup chain.
- Owner: A+B; milestone: W2/W10/W12.

## Scope creep

- Likelihood: High; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: New patterns/cloud/ML before gates.
- Prevention: Fixed Must/If stable/Defer tiers.
- Contingency: Record displaced work and cut stretch.
- Owner: A+B; milestone: Every gate.

## Late deployment

- Likelihood: High; impact: High; severity: High.
- Early warning: Host first appears in Week10.
- Prevention: Private real-host skeleton W2.
- Contingency: Block host gate now; do not substitute dev laptop.
- Owner: A; milestone: W2.

## Pattern over-engineering

- Likelihood: High; impact: Med; severity: Med.
- Early warning: Interfaces precede real pain.
- Prevention: Four yes admission and baseline first.
- Contingency: Keep simple method/switch and reject refactor.
- Owner: A+B; milestone: W3/W7/W9.

# Pattern learning path

## Admission before quota

Nine named candidates are reviewed, but only three have conditional lesson slots. No pattern is described as adopted in current application code. Source is unbuilt, so real pain cannot honestly be pre-certified. The target of seven to nine never overrides the admission test or critical gate schedule. DI and Repository are foundational explanations, not counted abstractions.

| Candidate | When | Outcome | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Builder | Week 3 | Conditional lesson | Two real fixture variations may justify named optional construction |
| Factory | Review Week 3 | Rejected now | No second configured provider exists |
| Strategy | Review Week 4 | Deferred | Critical attendance gate; simple calculation method first |
| Chain of Responsibility | Review Week 4 | Rejected now | Explicit validation order is clearer and safer |
| Adapter | Week 7 | Conditional lesson | Attachment disk/test isolation is a real requirement |
| Decorator | Review Week 5 | Rejected now | Framework transactions suffice; critical event gate |
| State and Template Method | Review Week 6/7 | Rejected now | Transition tables plus locked methods preserve distinct invariants |
| Specification | Week 9 | Conditional lesson | Admit only after two actual report filter combinations hurt |

State and Template Method are separate named candidates reviewed together; total named candidates is nine. Never add a pattern merely to reach the original target. No new refactors enter Week 11 hardening or Week 12 freeze.

## Lessons

- [Builder](03-ORGANIZATION-AND-ADMIN/PATTERN-LESSON.md).
- [Adapter](07-REQUESTS-AND-APPROVALS/PATTERN-LESSON.md).
- [Specification](09-REPORTING-AUDIT-OBSERVABILITY/PATTERN-LESSON.md).
- [Dependency injection primer](primers/DEPENDENCY-INJECTION.md).
- [Repository primer](primers/REPOSITORY.md).

Each conditional lesson uses one three-step stone: plain tested baseline, documented pain, then refactor with unchanged tests. A rejection completes the stone with a simpler tested implementation. No week exceeds two patterns or shares a new pattern with its riskiest critical gate.

# Definition of done

## Step

- [ ] One change takes 30 to 90 minutes, has a visible result, and has a focused commit.
- [ ] Any new term has a linked primer; at most two new concepts were introduced today.
- [ ] Expected result and failure recovery are checked; no secret is committed.

## Stone

- [ ] Required regression and negative tests pass with zero failures.
- [ ] Application startup and the stone's visible demonstration work.
- [ ] The final step's green tag points at the checked commit.
- [ ] A rejected pattern stays a simple method or switch; no quota-driven abstraction.

## Weekly gate

- [ ] Minimum Viable Gate evidence is recorded; Friday real-host redeploy and smoke pass.
- [ ] Backup exists on external media and a scratch restore was verified.
- [ ] Critical failures carry forward visibly; stretch is cut first.
- [ ] Thursday was buffer/review, weekend is rest, and next week's capacity is adjusted honestly.

## Release

- [ ] All Must checklist IDs have safe evidence, security and cross-tenant negatives included.
- [ ] Reboot, failed deploy, migration compatibility, secrets rotation and clean-host restore pass.
- [ ] HTTPS/auth/firewall/secrets/backup gate passed before external exposure.
- [ ] Known limitations and single-host outage risk are disclosed; guide completion is not product completion.

### 2.2 Reusable behavior profiles

Each endpoint entry below inherits the shared conventions and its named profile. These are normative parts of every entry, avoiding repeated security and transaction boilerplate.

| Profile | Headers and request | Success and response | Transaction, side effects, errors |
|---|---|---|---|
| READ | Bearer, correlation; no body | 200 named resource; ETag if mutable | Scoped owner/projection read; no events; common errors |
| LIST | READ plus endpoint filters and page/size/sort | 200 Page`<Resource>` | Scoped count and items; freshness if projected; no events |
| CREATE | Bearer, JSON, key | 201 resource + Location | Owner DB + audit + key result + listed outbox; 409/422 |
| CHANGE | Bearer, JSON, key, If-Match | 200 resource + new ETag | Lock current aggregate, authorize transition; atomic audit/outbox/key; 409/412/422/428 |
| EDIT | Bearer, JSON, If-Match | 200 resource + ETag | Typed update plus version increment/audit/outbox; retries use same precondition; 412/428 |
| REMOVE | Bearer, If-Match; no body | 204, no body | Soft delete/revoke and audit/outbox; repeat after disappearance 404; 412/428 |
| JOB | Bearer, JSON, key | 202 Job + Location=statusUrl | Persist owner job + key result; worker transaction later; 409/422 |
| MARK | Bearer, key; no version required | 200 receipt/resource | Monotonic own notification update; no business event; replay-safe |
| STREAM | Bearer, Accept:text/event-stream, Last-Event-ID optional | 200 event stream | Read own durable notifications; no mutation; reconnect reset on expired cursor |
| AUTH | Public JSON credential body; no key/If-Match | 200 Tokens | Rate-limited credential verification/refresh-family locking; 400/401/429/503 |

PATCH fields are the optional subset of the corresponding input schema unless a dedicated patch schema is named; required-on-create fields cannot be set null unless declared nullable. Path `{id}` and named IDs are UUID and must resolve within tenant/scope; `{code}` is an allowlisted template code. Unless listed otherwise, query parameters are none. Named list filters are optional and validated; unsupported filters return 400. Event names below refer to full catalog snapshots, not direct broker sends inside HTTP transactions.
